title: The Midpoint Transition
text:
For years, textbooks described team development as a steady march through stages. In the 1980s, Connie Gersick followed eight real project teams from their first meeting to their deadline to see what actually happened. They ranged from student groups to working teams inside organizations, with deadlines from about a week to six months.

Gersick watched and recorded their meetings. She found that each team settled on a basic approach to its work very early, often in the first meeting, and then stuck with it for a long time, even when it was not working well.

Then, at almost exactly the halfway point of the time they had, each team went through a burst of change. Members seemed to realize that time was running short. They dropped old patterns, sought outside input, and adopted a new approach. This happened at the calendar midpoint regardless of whether the project lasted a week or six months. The team then worked steadily on that new plan until a final push near the deadline. Gersick called the pattern punctuated equilibrium, borrowing a term from evolutionary biology.
lesson: Teams lock in their approach early and rethink it around the halfway mark. Use the first meeting and the midpoint deliberately to review direction.
source: Gersick, C. J. G. (1988). Time and transition in work teams: Toward a new model of group development. Academy of Management Journal, 31(1), 9-41.
